title: The bent made whole
hook: bend and be straight, empty and be full (Tao Te Ching 22)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was elusive and real: the Way, dim and slippery, with something true inside. Your line was something real.

A couch is stuck in a doorway. One person is in the hall, shoving. The other is inside the room, pulling. The couch doesn't move, and both of them are getting louder. Then a neighbor wanders past, looks for a second, and says, tilt it. Stand it on its end, turn it a little. The couch slides through as if the doorway had grown. Nobody got stronger. Somebody gave up the straight line. Chapter twenty-two of the Tao Te Ching is built on that moment, when bending is what gets the thing through.
screen: `A COUCH IN A DOORWAY.` → `SHOVE, PULL, NOTHING.` → `TILT IT.`

segments.voice: First, bent, then whole. The chapter opens with a run of reversals. In Legge's translation: "The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new." Each pair goes against common sense. We expect the bent thing to break. The chapter says the bent thing is the one that stays whole. Second, empty, then full. A cup that's already full can't receive; only an empty one can be filled. What is worn out makes room for what is new. Wanting follows the same pattern: whoever wants little, it says, gets it, and whoever wants a lot gets lost. Third, the sage doesn't push. Then the chapter turns to a person. The sage doesn't put himself on display, and so he shines. He doesn't insist he's right, and so he stands out. He doesn't boast, and so his work counts. He isn't proud of himself, and so he lasts. Fourth, no one can contend. Because the sage doesn't contend with anyone, the chapter says, no one in the world can contend with him. There's nothing to push against. It closes by asking whether the old saying about the bent being made whole was just empty words. Its answer: no. Becoming whole really comes this way. Yielding here isn't losing. It's how the couch gets through the door.
screen: `BENT, THEN WHOLE.` · `EMPTY, THEN FULL.` · `THE SAGE DOESN'T PUSH.` · `NO ONE CAN CONTEND.` · then, large: `THE CROOKED, STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small standoff: where the dishes go, which route to take, a comment you've been waiting to correct. Picture yourself saying fine, your way, and meaning it, and notice what happens in your shoulders. If it feels like losing, stay with it a moment longer.
Yield and be whole. Chapter twenty-two's run of reversals: the bent made whole, the empty filled, and the one who doesn't contend, whom no one can contend with. Today's word.
Your line: the bent is made whole. The one who doesn't contend leaves nothing to push against. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter twenty-two as a habit for daily life: giving way on small disagreements rather than pressing to win them.

Tao Te Ching.meaning: an ancient Chinese book of short chapters on the Way

Legge.meaning: James Legge, who translated the book into English in 1891

sage.meaning: a wise person; the book's picture of someone living the Way

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching, chapter 22 (few and many desires; the sage who does not display, justify, boast or pride himself; not contending; the ancients' saying)

notes: Verify the Legge 1891 wording: 'The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new.'

The rest of chapter 22 is paraphrased: few and many desires; the four 'doesn't ... and so ...' lines about the sage; 'because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him'; the closing claim that the ancients' saying is not empty words. Confirm.
The outline hook says 'bend and be straight'; the opening Chinese 曲則全 is more literally 'bent, then whole', and the 'crooked, straight' line follows. Both are covered.
The couch scene is an illustration, not a source.
Pronunciation guide for 曲則全 is approximate.
